Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $2$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068126/assets/c7b22b03b9952bfe068e9252f7336568aa8d761c32a1bc31c444ebb97ee925ba.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,0\cdot ({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\pi +0 \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
